query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of molybdenum (~5 at.%) to the titanium‐ and nickel‐rich, single‐phase solid‐solution HEA will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor molybdenum addition (around 5 atomic percent) during alloy synthesis so that Mo becomes a major part of the composition rather than a mere trace addition.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and creep tests) in the range of 800°C to 1200°C, with appropriate aging experiments in an inert or controlled atmosphere to limit oxidation and impurity pickup.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to promote a refined microstructure through enhanced solid-solution and precipitation strengthening. It may lead to the formation of coherent nano-precipitates and reduce grain boundary mobility, thereby retarding grain growth and impurity-induced softening at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Molybdenum increases the overall lattice stability by raising the effective melting point and strengthening the atomic bonding. Its presence enhances solid-solution strengthening and may favor the nucleation of fine precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, both critical at elevated temperatures. It may also help to ‘scavenge’ impurity interstitials (e.g., oxygen/nitrogen) that otherwise promote local compositional fluctuations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the molybdenum-modified HEA will exhibit increased yield strength, better creep resistance, and overall improved mechanical stability when subjected to high-temperature or extreme-environment testing.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-based HEA produced without the Mo addition, which is anticipated to show lower elevated-temperature strength and a tendency toward softening upon extended thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Ti–Ni dominant HEAs maintained as single-phase solid solutions; the beneficial effect of Mo is expected as long as its content remains at a level that does not induce detrimental secondary phase formation. Testing should be performed under inert or reducing atmospheres and within the temperature window typical for high-temperature applications (approximately 800°C–1200°C).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo level and its precise role in precipitate formation or impurity control are not fully established. The interaction between Mo and inherent impurities or other trace elements could modulate the effect, so further detailed microstructural characterization is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloy samples using identical processing conditions: one set of the base Ti–Ni HEA and a second set with an additional ~5 at.% Mo. Subject both sets to elevated-temperature mechanical test protocols (tensile and creep tests) at several temperatures within 800°C to 1200°C over various hold times. Perform detailed microstructural analysis (using XRD, SEM/TEM) to check for the formation of any deleterious phases and to assess grain size stability.
measurements: Yield strength, creep rate, and microhardness at the specified elevated temperatures
Microstructural features such as precipitate size/distribution and grain boundary character
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-enhanced alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, at least a 10% higher yield strength or appreciably slower creep rate) relative to the control, or if adverse secondary phases form that compromise the intended improvement, the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
